clinical_targets.goal: Complete alleviation of primary presenting complaint and systemic stability
Return of baseline physiological parameters (vital signs, CBC, metabolic panel)
Full return to activities of daily living (ADLs) and functional autonomy

steps_summary: Step 1: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
Step 3: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
Step 4: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Malnutrition focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.role: Standard initial therapy for mild-to-moderate Malnutrition.
drug_classes.dosing: Initiate standard therapeutic dosing; titrate over 2–4 weeks based on clinical response and tolerability.
drug_classes.pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Dose optimization and complementary therapeutic escalation.
drug_classes.dosing: Titrate to target clinical biomarker thresholds under specialist guidance.
drug_classes.pearls: Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Malnutrition require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Malnutrition.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Calculate CrCl using Cockcroft-Gault before prescribing narrow therapeutic index drugs.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Review patient's complete prescription and OTC medication list for drug-induced liver injury (DILI).
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Verify safety in pregnancy and lactation databases before prescribing any new therapeutic class.
special_populations.elderly: Perform medication reconciliation to eliminate unnecessary polypharmacy and anticholinergic load.

style_3_monograph.summary: What is malnutrition? Malnutrition means that your body isn't getting enough calories or the right balance of nutrients to stay healthy. This can happen if you don't get enough protein , carbohydrates , and fats , eat too much unhealthy food, or don't get the vitamins and minerals your body needs. Malnutrition can affect people of all ages, but children, older adults, and people with chronic (long-term) health problems have a higher risk. What are the types of malnutrition? Most people think of undernutrition with malnutrition. But malnutrition can refer to undernutrition, overnutrition, or an imbalance of nutrients. Types of malnutrition include: Protein-energy undernutrition , also called macronutrient undernutrition, happens when your body doesn't get enough protein or calories from food. Two serious forms of this are kwashiorkor and marasmus. An imbalanced nutritional status occurs when you are not getting the right mix of nutrients. You may get enough calories, but not enough vitamins or minerals. Vitamin deficiency diseases happen when your body doesn't get enough of certain vitamins. Without the right vitamins, your body cannot stay healthy and may develop specific diseases. For example, scurvy can develop from too little vitamin C , rickets from too little vitamin D , and anemia from too little iron or vitamin B12 . Faltering weight occurs when children don't gain weight or grow as expected . This may be due to not getting enough food, trouble absorbing nutrients , or other health problems. Overnutrition can occur when your body gets too many calories or nutrients. This may lead to obesity or other health issues. What causes malnutrition? Malnutrition may occur for many reasons, including: An unbalanced diet that lacks variety or specific nutrients Some medical issues, which could include malabsorption syndromes, dementia , eating disorders , depression , alcohol use disorder (AUD) , or cancer Problems with swallowing, digestion, or dental issues Certain medicines that affect how food tastes and smells Not being able to get food or cook due to things such as chronic illness, mobility issues, or low income Who is at risk for developing malnutrition? Malnutrition can affect anyone, but some people have a higher risk than others. This includes people who: Don't have enough knowledge about nutrition Don't have access to a variety of food Are older adults or children Have a low income Have a chronic (long-term) illness What are the symptoms of malnutrition? The symptoms of malnutrition can vary. You may have no symptoms, but if you do, they may include: Fatigue and weakness Dizziness Losing weight without trying Low body weight Slow growth or development in children Frequent infections or slow healing Dry skin or brittle hair and nails Swelling in the legs, feet, or belly How is malnutrition diagnosed? To check for malnutrition, your health care provider may: Do a nutritional screening , which may include questions about weight loss, changes in your appetite, and your ability to eat Do a physical exam and order blood tests to check for signs that you don't have enough nutrients Refer you to other providers that specialize in nutrition, such as a dietician What are the treatments for malnutrition? Treatment for malnutrition may include improving your diet, replacing missing nutrients, and treating the underlying cause. Can malnutrition be prevented? To help prevent malnutrition, eat a healthy diet with many different foods. Talk with your provider if you are worried about your diet, weight loss, or your child's growth.
style_3_monograph.treatment: The goal of treatment is to replace the thiamine your body is lacking. This is done with thiamine supplements. Thiamine supplements are given through a shot (injection) or taken by mouth. Your provider may also suggest other types of vitamins. Blood tests may be repeated after the treatment is started. These tests will show how well you are responding to the medicine.
